draw.question: After the power returns, within what time window should you restock everything used during the outage, and which two items should you restock first?
draw.expectedAnswer: Restock everything used during the outage within one week, starting with water and batteries.

draw.question: Perishable food that has spent how long above what temperature should be discarded?
draw.expectedAnswer: Any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius should be discarded.

draw.question: For how long does refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remain usable at room temperature, and who should you confirm the rule with for your specific medication?
draw.expectedAnswer: Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist.

draw.question: In cold weather, which room in the home should you gather everyone in, and what is stated to be safer than any improvised heater?
draw.expectedAnswer: Choose one small room on a south-facing side of the home ... layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater.

draw.question: Besides keeping both refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible, what specific reminder action does the guide instruct?
draw.expectedAnswer: Tape a note to each door as a reminder.

draw.question: How many battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms should you install, and on which floors?
draw.expectedAnswer: Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.

draw.question: Which six non-perishable foods does the guide name as good choices for the emergency shelf?
draw.expectedAnswer: Canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk.

draw.question: For about how long does an unopened refrigerator keep food safe?
draw.expectedAnswer: An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours.

=== STEP 1 · NUMBERED FACTS FROM ORIGINAL artifact/GUIDE.md ===
Body split into sentences on '.', '!', '?' in reading order; every sentence stating a checkable fact indexed from F1.
F1: outage lasting up to seventy-two hours.
F2: written for a temperate climate and assumes no backup generator.
F3: work through the sections in order; earlier sections cover the preparations that matter most.
F4: store four litres of water per person per day = twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours.
F5: half of that allowance for drinking, the other half for cooking and basic hygiene.
F6: store water in food-grade containers, out of direct sunlight, replace every six months.
F7: if a storm is forecast with advance warning, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking.
F8: dedicated shelf of non-perishable food sufficient for three days.
F9: good choices: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, shelf-stable milk.
F10: choose foods requiring no cooking; own a manual can opener (electric useless).
F11: eat perishable refrigerator food first, then freezer, then the emergency shelf.
F12: an unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours.
F13: full freezer holds safe temperature about forty-eight hours, half-full only about twenty-four hours.
F14: keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a note to each door as a reminder.
F15: discard perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius.
F16: use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as primary light; avoid candles (leading cause of house fires during outages).
F17: store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each light.
F18: one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen.
F19: never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window (carbon monoxide, odourless, can be fatal).
F20: install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.
F21: in cold, choose one small room on a south-facing side, close its door, gather everyone; layered clothing and blankets safer than any improvised heater.
F22: if indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or neighbour's home.
F23: keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio; know the frequency of your local emergency station before the outage.
F24: a full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours recharges a typical phone roughly four times.
F25: put your phone in low-power mode at the start; agree in advance on one out-of-area contact everyone texts.
F26: keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotate to stay in date.
F27: refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature up to twenty-eight days; confirm with a pharmacist.
F28: write pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control numbers on paper.
F29: wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on.
F30: if freezer food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen.
F31: restock everything used during the outage within one week, starting with water and batteries.
F32: write a one-page note about what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.
Total facts: 32 (F1..F32).
